id: messenger-audio/53 Quran Study 22 Oct 1982 By Dr Rashad Khalifa - Original
title: MA 53 — Quran Study (Dr. Rashad Khalifa, 10/22/1982) [Original]

chapters.title: Bad Muslims and the Case Against Islam
chapters.description: The recording opens mid-argument. Dean Mahmoud presses the question of whether the failings of Muslims discredit Islam itself, and a graduate student answers from the book the group has been reading: after the Mongol invasion the universities that survived taught only hadith, sunna and jurisprudence, so algebra, Greek philosophy and free thought were driven out of the curriculum and replaced by the repetition of old material.
chapters.speaker: Dean Mahmoud

chapters.title: Ninety Percent Rejected as Untrustworthy
chapters.description: On the compilers of hadith: for two hundred years after the Prophet's death they rejected ninety percent of what reached them as untrustworthy, and Dean Mahmoud adds that even those who kept the remaining tenth doubted it. The parallel drawn is Christianity, where the word of the Pope became equivalent to the word of God and church doctrine displaced the teachings of Christ. One consolation offered: the group has no organised clergy.
chapters.speaker: Dr. Khalifa

chapters.title: A Thesis on the Probability of the Quran
chapters.description: A student in his first semester of an engineering programme floats a Master's thesis topic: a numerical analysis of the Quran showing that the probability of a book being produced this way lies beyond human capacity. The conversation turns on the observation that engineering decisions rest on probability rather than certainty, and that statistics is the first thing one studies in order to decide anything at all.
chapters.speaker: A man

chapters.title: Doing Good: Humanist Versus Quranic Grounds
chapters.description: Dean Mahmoud draws the distinction that gives the discussion its shape. From a humanistic point of view, doing good for society is an end in itself; from the Quranic point of view one does good because God commanded it, which makes it a duty rather than a preference. The students name the alternative they see around them as utilitarian or pragmatic ethics, where in a highly industrialised society whatever makes money counts as what is good.
chapters.speaker: Dean Mahmoud

chapters.title: "Why Don't You Go to God?"
chapters.description: Khalifa notes that God has nothing against the Prophet but tells us not to follow his behaviour. A student then relates an exchange from a Quran class at the MSA, where a speaker had retreated to the position that the hadith are not divine revelation like the Quran, and had said that when he does not understand the Quran he goes to the hadith for interpretation. The student's wife answered: why go to the hadith, why don't you go to God? Khalifa calls it exactly the point, and adds that the books of hadith were written by people of different backgrounds and nationalities, which makes them harder to interpret rather than easier.
chapters.speaker: A man

chapters.title: Consumer Mentality in 1982 America
chapters.description: The longest single statement of the first half. A student calls the instilling of a consumer mentality through television and the media vulgar: from the day a person begins watching to the day he dies he is encouraged to buy, whether or not he needs it. He names it super hyper materialism, unprecedented in that the great mass of people can now consume at a level never before possible, and argues that short-sightedness also explains the pace of nuclear development. Dean Mahmoud closes the informal half with the reminder that work is a part of worship.
chapters.speaker: A man

chapters.title: Al-Fatiha and Al-Baqarah: The Three Groups
chapters.description: The study proper begins, and Khalifa opens it by thanking God for enlightening the group through Dean Mahmoud, whose discovery the previous week he calls a tremendous parallelism. The three descriptions that close Al-Fatiha at 1:7 map onto the three groups Al-Baqarah then sets out in detail: those whom You blessed are the righteous, those who deserved wrath are the disbelievers, and the strayers are the hypocrites. Khalifa reports that people have told him it gives them a wholly new perspective when reciting Al-Fatiha, and notes that the strayers are so named because a person can only stray from a path he was once on.
chapters.speaker: Dr. Khalifa

chapters.title: Written Before Creation, Revealed on Occasion
chapters.description: Khalifa draws the conclusion he considers watertight: thirteen years and some two hundred miles separate the revelation of Sura 1 from Sura 2, so a connection this tight proves the Quran was written down before the creation of the heavens and the earth, then released piece by piece as occasions arose. His examples are the passage on the Prophet turning away and frowning from the blind poor man, and the description of the battle of Badr, each written before the earth existed and revealed immediately after the event.
chapters.speaker: Dr. Khalifa

chapters.title: Dean Mahmoud on 1:6 and the Hypocrites as a Subset
chapters.description: Dean Mahmoud offers his own week's work, prefacing it by saying he is not pushing it because he is not sure of it himself. First on 1:6, where he traces the root behind the straight path through ordinary and Quranic dictionaries and concludes that the root originally carried straightness and righteousness together, so the verse can be read as a plea for guidance on the path of righteousness. Then his main argument: the hypocrites are not a separate group but a subset of the disbelievers, established from 2:8, where those who say they believe are declared not to be believers, and from 2:19. In the language of mathematics, all hypocrites are disbelievers but not all disbelievers are hypocrites, so 2:8 should be read as "then there are those [among the disbelievers] who say...". He observes that Zamakhshari, Baydawi and al-Manar all laboured over the difference between those who deserve wrath and those who stray, and none of them noticed that the answer sits on the next page. The session ends on why the strayers occupy the hottest part of Hell: they were on the path, so they have no excuse.
chapters.speaker: Dean Mahmoud
